title: Appendix A — Draft: Data Documentation
text:
Goal is to give evidence to my boss that shark-infested storms are very rare, if not impossible.
The data I found is from the NOAA data base. I extracted tornado data from Los Angeles (the setting of Sharknado), Florida (tropical storms are abundant), South Carolina (another more tropical place), and Oklahoma (the tornado capitol of the nation).
All the data sets are the same format. They were collected from the same data base NOAA.gov.
These are the important aspects of the data sets collected

County Location
Begin Location
Begin Date
Begin Time
Tornado F Scale
Direct Deaths
Direct Injuries
Property Damage
Tornado Length and Width
End Location
End Date
End Time

Measurements are take by the MWS Storm Survey, Spotters, State officials and the Public

Florida tornado data: “Storm Events Database - Search Results  National Centers for Environmental Information” (n.d.a)
South Carolina tornado data: “Storm Events Database - Search Results  National Centers for Environmental Information” (n.d.b)
Oklahoma tornado data: “Storm Events Database - Search Results  National Centers for Environmental Information” (n.d.c)
Los Angeles tornado data: “Storm Events Database - Search Results  National Centers for Environmental Information” (n.d.d)

For a tornado to lift up a Shark I compared the weight of a Great White Shark to a normal cars weight

Great White Shark Weight

NOAA Says up to 4,500 lbs

Car weight

According to autoinsurance.com a Car SUV is 3,986 lbs
According to autoinsurance.com a Truck SUV is 4,578 lbs

Great White Sharks and Car SUVs and Truck SUVs weigh relatively around the same weight.

oteroadjusting.com says EF3 tornadoes are likely to toss cars and trucks and EF5 can “almost certainly lift and destroy cars.”
I will use this as a reference to say that EF3-EF5 tornadoes will be able to lift a great white shark.

title: Appendix B — Draft: Results
text:
Note



The language you’re using is a bit narrative and informal - can you make it slightly more professional
“A Sharknado event requires that a shark is picked up from the ocean by a tornado and deposited inland. We first consider the physics: how much does a shark weigh, and what types of objects do tornadoes regularly disrupt? What strength of tornado is required in order to lift an object as heavy as a shark?” <then, add your logic, which is great>
“This report considers tornadoes between 2015 and 2026 occurring in four states which were chosen because of specific characteristics which may impact the probability of a sharknado event occurring. ”
It is a bit odd to consider LA specifically instead of California?
Don’t show code or messages/warnings.
Lots of grammar mistakes – subject/verb agreement, tense – “There has been nine EF3 tornadoes with one EF4 tornado”
Should you use a table or perhaps consider a stacked bar chart to show the distribution of tornado strength across the regions you are considering? What would be more effective? Your figure looks reasonable to me, but the color scheme is a bit … icky. Choose something that has a monochrome gradient, since the EF scale has a specific meaning and order.
All tables and figures should have captions and labels and be referenced in the text.
“Let’s take a look” is a reasonable thing in a user guide but is too casual for a business report.
If you remove the PDF format from the _quarto.yml file, I think your references will work better.
Summarize your results appropriately in a callout box for skimmability.
Also, an EF1 tornado isn’t supposed to be able to destroy buildings enough to be able to grab a shark from an aquarium. So that’s hardly proof of anything. LMK when an aquarium is obliterated in Oklahoma or something. :) (actually, https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2015/may/06/oklahoma-tornado-severe-weather-texas-kansas-nebraska is relevant – but the tigers escaped because of the damage and don’t seem to have been picked up by the storm itself).


A Sharknado event involves a tornado being able to lift a great white shark out of the ocean and carry it onto land. To see if this is possible, we need to look at the physics: the weight of a great white shark, what objects are known to be picked up by tornadoes, and the magnitude of tornadoes required to pick up a shark. First, we need to find out how a great white shark could be picked up by a tornado. We will be looking at the weight of a great white shark first and comparing it to other objects that can and have been picked up by tornadoes, such as cars. Next, figuring out what strength (in EF scale from EF3 - EF5) of a tornado would be needed to be able to lift a great white shark and a car. Lastly, we are going to look at some tornadoes from 2015-2026 that are in the desired EF scale range (EF3-EF5) from 4 different places in the United States. These places are going to be Florida, South Carolina, Oklahoma, California, and Los Angeles. These places were chosen for specific reasons. Florida has many tropical storms and is a coastal state (Florida, (n.d.)). South Carolina is also another place that can be hit by tropical storms and is another coastal state (South Carolina, (n.d.)). Oklahoma is not a coastal state, but it is the tornado capital of the United States, so we will just look at the number of tornadoes that meet our criteria (Oklahoma, (n.d.)). California ((n.d.)) was chosen because it is the state setting of Sharknado, while Los Angeles ((n.d.)) was picked because it is the city setting of the Sharknado movie.
Sharks and cars weigh relatively the same in pounds (lbs). The average great white shark weighs around 4,500 lbs (Fisheries (2025)). A car SUV weighs around 3,986 lbs while a truck SUV weighs around 4,578 lbs (AutoInsurance (n.d.)). This means that your average great white shark weighs more than a big car and as much as a truck or SUV. We will use a car as the base to find what EF scale level will be used to lift a great white shark out of the water.
The EF scale is made up of 6 different ratings of tornado based on 3-second wind speed in mph (US Department of Commerce (n.d.)). An EF0 tornado is has the lowest wind speed ranging between 65-85 mph, EF1 has winds speeds between 86-110 mph, EF2 has wind speeds between 111-135 mph, EF3 has wind speeds of 136-165 mph, EF4 has speeds between 166-200 mph and EF5 has wind speed that are over 200 mph. An EF3 tornado is likely to toss cars and trucks, while an EF4 is very likely to toss cars many feet, and an EF5 tornado is almost certain to lift and destroy cars. Since we are comparing a great white shark to the size and weight of a car SUV and a truck SUV, that gives us a good comparison to be able to put a shark in the place of those cars in the EF scales’ ability to lift cars (Quach (2025)). We are going to look at tornadoes that are only EF3 to EF5 because those are the strength of tornadoes that are able to lift a car (Salaita (n.d.)).
Let’s take a look at some tornado data from a tropical place that gets some pretty bad storms regularly in Florida. Florida is also a place that is on the coast, so it would be able to pick up a shark in the event of a strong enough tornado.

library(tidyverse)

  select(STATE_ABBR, EVENT_TYPE, TOR_F_SCALE, BEGIN_LAT, BEGIN_LON)|>

Figure B.1: Florida Higher Than EF2 Tornado Data




Figure B.1 shows that there have been only 5 EF3 tornadoes in the last 10 years in the state of Florida. Because of an EF3 tornado being the highest EF rating, and it being “likely to toss a car or truck” we can believe that a tornado in Florida is pretty unlikely to pick up the average great white shark. Having only five EF3 tornadoes in the past 10 years seems like the chances of a Sharknado happening look pretty slim. Below is a map showing these tornadoes.


Code
fl_map <- map_data("state") |>
  filter(region == "florida")

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = fl_map, 
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "gray90", color = "black") +
  
  geom_point(data = tornado_fl,
             aes(x = BEGIN_LON, y = BEGIN_LAT, color = TOR_F_SCALE),
             size = 2, alpha = .5)+
  theme_minimal()








Figure B.2: Florida Higher Than EF2 Tornado Map





Figure B.2 shows a map of Florida showing the five EF3 tornadoes that have occurred in the last 10 years. There is one tornado that shows up close to the water, but looking at the coordinates, it appears on the beach. EF3 tornadoes are likely to toss cars and trucks (Quach (2025)). Tossing and picking up are not the same thing in this scenario, so an EF3 tornado is not very likely to fully pick up a shark.

South Carolina is similar to Florida from Figure B.3. There are a lot of EF3 tornadoes with one EF4 tornado. But it’s in the same boat as Florida; there has been a very limited number of powerful tornadoes over the past 10 years in South Carolina. There have been nine EF3 tornadoes and one EF4 tornado over that span. The surprising thing is that the EF4 and six of the EF3 tornadoes all happened on the same day. But the possibility of a Sharknado is very low because these tornadoes all happened away from the coast. The EF4 happened in Estill and Hampton Counties (Climatology Office (2020)). Below is a map showing all the tornadoes from South Carolina over the last 10 years.

The EF4 tornado is the main Sharknado threat. As seen in Figure B.4, all tornadoes EF3 and above only appear on land and are far enough from the coast to have any real threat of a Sharknado. From the evidence from Florida and now South Carolina, a Sharknado is looking less and less possible.

By comparing the levels of EF ratings specified before (needing between EF3 - EF5), we can see there is not really a possibility of getting a tornado with wind speeds strong enough to pick up a shark to create a Sharknado. Note that California only has EF0 and EF1 tornadoes, so we will use those only in this chart.


Code

  tornado_fl,
  tornado_sc,
  tornado_ok_10,
  tornado_ca_10
)

  geom_bar()+
    scale_fill_discrete(
    name = "Tornado Strength",
    labels = c("EF0","EF1","EF3","EF4","EF5")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10,by = 2)) +
  theme_minimal()








Figure B.9: Bar Chart for Tornadoes Higher than EF3 Over Last 10 Years for FL, SC, and OK, All Tornadoes Over Last 10 Years for CA





Figure B.9 allows us to look at the strength of each location’s tornadoes on the EF scale compared to each other. The wind speed needed to lift a shark off the ground is 200 mph (Salaita (n.d.)). An EF3 tornado has wind speeds of 136-165 mph, an EF4 tornado has speeds between 166-200 mph, and an EF5 tornado has wind speeds that are over 200 mph. This means that an EF5 tornado is only strong enough to lift a shark off the ground. It is shown that there have only been two tornadoes in the last ten years that have been strong enough to have wind speeds of 200 mph or more. So there were only two tornadoes that were strong enough to be able to pick up a shark, but they happened in Oklahoma. That means there is no chance that there is a possibility that a Sharknado can happen in Florida, South Carolina, or Los Angeles. But in Oklahoma, there might be a possibility of a Sharknado. At the Oklahoma Aquarium in Jenks, OK, there is Shark Adventure, which is home to ten of the “most dangerous sharks known to man” (Aquarium (n.d.)). These sharks are bull sharks. Jenks, OK, is in Tulsa County, so let’s look at some tornadoes over the last 10 years for Tulsa County, Oklahoma.

Figure B.10 shows all tornadoes that have gone through Tulsa County, Oklahoma, and shows that these tornadoes don’t reach EF3 or higher at all. But Bull Sharks only weigh around 500 lbs (“Bull Shark. National Wildlife Federation” (n.d.)). This means that they are much easier for a tornado to lift up than a great white shark. An EF2 tornado has the strength to slightly move houses off their foundations and destroy mobile homes (“The Weighty Truth: How Much Can a Tornado Lift? - Oreate AI Blog” (2025)). If an EF2 tornado went through the Oklahoma Aquarium in Jenks and destroyed the aquarium, it could potentially pick up sharks from the “most dangerous sharks known to man” exhibit to create a real-life Sharknado. Thinking of this logic, this could also apply to a lot of other aquariums throughout the country. But the chances of this happening are relatively low. The last time a tornado hit an aquarium was in 2024 when an EF1 tornado went through the Pittsburgh Zoo & Aquarium (Shannon (2024)). This only resulted in little damage to the property and some trees being knocked over. This means that an EF1 tornado going through a zoo/aquarium will not cause enough damage to destroy buildings and have wind speeds strong enough to pick up objects as heavy as a shark. Thinking about the possibility of a Sharknado is pretty slim when there is a record of a tornado that went through an aquarium; there was still no chance.
Just thinking with the insurance payout possibilities in mind, storms and tornadoes that are not shark-infested will still cause property damage. Storms and tornadoes with high wind speeds and storms with varying precipitation types and amounts are still possible and can still cause massive amounts of property damage. Sharknados may be out of the picture, but there are many other ways that weather-related events can cause property damage.

title: Appendix C — Draft: Intro/Conclusions
text:
D Introduction
This study goes over the idea the possibility of a Sharknado scenario for insurance payouts for property damage purposes. A Sharknado is explained by a tornado that generates enough wind speed to be able to lift a heavy animal, such as a great white shark, out of the water and into its vortex. A Sharknado can also be called a “Shark infested tornado”.
This study starts by comparing the average great white shark to objects of similar weight specifically cars or pickup trucks. Tornadoes are known for destroying homes and tossing around vehicles thus finding the types of vehicles that are similar enough in weight to a great white shark makes finding the right magnitude of tornadoes required to lift a great white shark easier.
Next, finding the magnitude of a tornado capable of picking up a great white shark, or a car, is found using the EF scale (Enhanced Fujita Scale) by looking at EF ratings (US Department of Commerce (n.d.)). The Enhanced Fujita Scale uses rating of EF0 to EF5. Tornadoes of interest for this study are tornadoes of rating EF3 to EF5. These tornadoes have strong enough wind speeds to potentially pick up and throw cars or, in this case, a great white shark.
Finally, looking at places that are near the coast to be able to pick up a great white shark is essential to actually generating a Sharknado. There are 3 locations observed for their tornado data that fit this agenda in this study. Those places being Florida, South Carolina, and Los Angeles (this is the setting of the Sharknado movie). For another comparison of tornado strength Oklahoma is also looked at for tornado EF rating. These locations are have tornado data taken from 2015 - 2026 using NOAA tornado data.
By combining the magnitude of tornadoes with the areas where these tornadoes touched down gives an idea to the possibility of a potential Sharknado event occurring.

title: Appendix D — Draft: Executive Summary
text:
E Executive Summary

E.0.1 Purpose of Report
This study dives into the possibility of a Sharknado event. A Sharknado can be explained as a “shark infested tornado”. This is a tornado that generates enough wind speed to lift a great white shark from the water and into its vortex. The purpose of this study is to assess a Sharknado event could be considered as a risk for property damage insurance pay outs.


E.0.2 Methods
To start, a comparison of the weight of a great white shark (around 4500 lbs) and vehicles (around 4000 - 4600 lbs for SUV and Trucks) is used because cars are known to be lifted and destroyed by tornadoes. Using the EF (Enhanced Fujita) Scale the strength of tornado able to lift and toss cars (or a great white shark) is found to be between EF3 - EF5 tornadoes. This is wind speeds of 136 mph to 200+ mph. This study will only be looking at tornadoes of EF3 - EF5 because of this reason. This study also looks at four locations of tornado data from 2015-2026. These locations are Florida, South Carolina, Oklahoma, California, and Los Angeles County, CA. These places were chosen because of their abundant tropical storms and coastal area (Florida and South Carolina), historic tornado amounts and strength (Oklahoma), and the setting of the movie Sharknado (Los Angeles, CA).


E.0.3 Findings
Tornadoes of strength EF3 - EF5 are fairly uncommon for coastal states like Florida, and South Carolina. Florida had only five tornadoes in the last 10 years that are of strength EF3 and zero EF4 and EF5 tornadoes. All but one of these tornadoes are started started and ended on land. The one tornado other tornado started on a beach in Florida where the water is not deep enough for sharks. South Carolina had nine EF3 and one EF4 tornado over the last 10 years. All of these tornadoes started and stayed on land making a Sharknado impossible. Oklahoma has had plenty of tornadoes strong enough to lift and carry a shark but there are no sharks in Oklahoma besides in the Oklahoma Aquarium in Jenks, OK. California has not had a tornado above an EF2 over the last 10 years.


E.0.4 Conclusions
The probability of a Sharknado event is extremely low, if not a zero percent chance. There was one tornado in the three coastal states that might have had the ability to lift a shark. This South Carolina tornado happened to start and end on land making a Sharknado impossible. The Oklahoma Aquarium houses sharks in a state that is known for its amount and strengths of tornadoes. The Oklahoma Aquarium is in Tulsa County, OK where only EF2 or lower tornadoes have touched down in the last 10 years rendering this as very improbable.


E.0.5 Recommendations
From this study it is fairly certain that Sharknado’s are extremely unlikely if not a zero percent chance. Even though, strong storms and tornadoes without sharks are still a cause for concern. Property damage and their resulting insurance payouts will still be present with storms and tornadoes that have high wind speeds and with precipitaion events
